metadata.title: AWS IAM — Decision Intelligence Knowledge Base
metadata.description: Production IAM patterns: least privilege, role assumption, cross-account access, IRSA, permission boundaries, and policy authoring rules.
source_alignment: CIS AWS Foundations Benchmark v3.0 — Section 1 (Identity and Access Management)
AWS re:Invent SEC sessions — Cross-Account Access Patterns

entries.concept: Users vs Roles vs Federated Identity
entries.description: IAM users are long-lived credentials and should be the exception, not the rule. Roles are short-lived assumed credentials issued by STS and are the correct primitive for workloads, cross-account access, and human SSO. Federated identity (IAM Identity Center / SSO with SAML or OIDC) replaces IAM users for human access. The identity model decides everything downstream: rotation, audit, blast radius.
decision_rules: USE IAM Identity Center (SSO) for all human access — federated, MFA-enforced, group-mapped, no static keys
USE IAM roles for all workloads (EC2 instance profile, ECS task role, EKS IRSA, Lambda execution role)
AVOID creating IAM users except for: (a) emergency break-glass, (b) third-party tools that cannot federate
ROTATE any unavoidable IAM access keys every 90 days max; alert on keys older than 180 days
REQUIRE MFA on all IAM users and on the root account; root credentials must be vaulted and never used for daily ops
tradeoffs: Roles + STS: ephemeral and audited but require trust-policy management and assume-role boilerplate
IAM Identity Center: centralized but adds a dependency on AWS Organizations and SSO config
Long-lived users: simple but high blast radius on credential leak
anti_patterns: Embedding IAM access keys in CI variables or Dockerfiles — use OIDC federation to AWS instead
Sharing IAM users between humans — destroys audit trail
Using the root account for any operation other than billing and account-level setup
Creating one IAM role per service AND attaching AdministratorAccess as a 'temporary' fix

entries.concept: Writing least-privilege policies that survive review
entries.description: Least privilege means starting from zero permissions and adding only what is provably required. Production policies must scope by Action, Resource, and Condition. Wildcards in Resource are the single largest source of accidental privilege escalation. AWS provides Access Analyzer (Policy Generation) which generates policies from CloudTrail history — the recommended starting point for any non-trivial role.
decision_rules: GENERATE candidate policies with IAM Access Analyzer Policy Generation from 90 days of CloudTrail
SCOPE every Action to specific Resource ARNs — `Resource: "*"` is allowed only for genuinely global APIs (e.g. ec2:DescribeRegions)
USE Conditions for defense-in-depth: aws:SourceVpc, aws:SourceIp, aws:PrincipalOrgID, aws:RequestTag
USE permission boundaries on roles created by developers — boundary caps the maximum reachable privilege
DENY wins — use explicit Deny statements as guardrails (e.g. deny iam:* outside a specific admin role)
TAG roles and use ABAC (`aws:ResourceTag/Project`) for multi-team accounts to keep policies short
tradeoffs: Strict scoping: high security but more policy churn when new resources appear — mitigate with ABAC
Permission boundaries: protect against privilege escalation but add cognitive load for engineers
Service Control Policies (SCPs) at the org level: blunt but powerful guardrail vs per-account complexity
anti_patterns: `Action: "*", Resource: "*"` — that is AdministratorAccess by another name
Attaching `*FullAccess` AWS-managed policies to workload roles — they are too broad for production
Using `iam:PassRole` with `Resource: "*"` — enables privilege escalation via Lambda/EC2/ECS
Skipping Conditions — a policy without `aws:SourceVpc` or `aws:PrincipalOrgID` is exploitable from any account that gets the credentials

entries.concept: AssumeRole with ExternalId for third-party and cross-account
entries.description: Cross-account access is implemented with an IAM role in the target account whose trust policy permits a principal in a different account (or third-party AWS account) to call sts:AssumeRole. For third-party access, the trust policy MUST require an `sts:ExternalId` known only to the third party — this prevents the confused-deputy attack where another customer of the same vendor could assume your role.
decision_rules: REQUIRE sts:ExternalId in the trust policy of any role assumable by a third-party AWS account
GENERATE a unique, high-entropy ExternalId per integration; never reuse across customers or roles
SCOPE the trust policy Principal to a specific account ID, not aws:PrincipalOrgID, when integrating with vendors
USE aws:PrincipalOrgID in trust policies for INTRA-organization access — it auto-trusts all member accounts
SET role session duration to the minimum that completes the job (default 1h, max 12h)
LOG all sts:AssumeRole calls and alert on unexpected source accounts
tradeoffs: Short session duration: better security vs more refresh churn for long-running jobs
PrincipalOrgID trust: scales with org growth but trusts every account — pair with SCPs
Per-vendor unique role: clean blast radius vs more roles to manage
anti_patterns: Trust policy with `Principal: "*"` — any AWS account in the world can assume the role
Reusing the same ExternalId across multiple vendors — defeats the confused-deputy mitigation
Granting cross-account access by sharing IAM access keys instead of using AssumeRole
Allowing the role to call sts:AssumeRole on itself or a more privileged role (chained escalation)

entries.concept: IAM Roles for Service Accounts (IRSA) on EKS
entries.description: IRSA binds a Kubernetes ServiceAccount to an IAM role via OIDC federation. Pods using that ServiceAccount receive short-lived, automatically-rotated AWS credentials with exactly the role's permissions. IRSA replaces the older anti-patterns of (a) attaching IAM permissions to the entire node, and (b) baking access keys into pods. It is the only correct way to give a pod AWS access in production.
decision_rules: ENABLE the cluster OIDC provider and create per-application IAM roles bound to per-application ServiceAccounts
SCOPE the role's trust policy to the exact `system:serviceaccount:<ns>:<sa>` subject — not the whole cluster
STRIP node-level IAM permissions to the absolute minimum (ECR pull, CNI, autoscaler) — never put app permissions on the node role
USE one role per workload — never share an IRSA role across distinct applications or namespaces
PAIR IRSA with NetworkPolicy and PodSecurityStandard restricted — IRSA only covers AWS API access, not in-cluster access
tradeoffs: Per-workload roles: clean blast radius vs more roles and trust policies to manage (Terraform module helps)
IRSA: cleanest workload identity vs requires OIDC provider setup; alternative is Pod Identity (newer, simpler)
EKS Pod Identity (2023+): simpler than IRSA, no OIDC required, but cluster-scoped agent dependency
anti_patterns: Attaching application-specific IAM permissions to the node IAM role — every pod on the node inherits them
Mounting AWS credentials as a Kubernetes Secret — long-lived, no automatic rotation
Using a single 'app' ServiceAccount across all workloads — defeats per-workload least privilege
Trust policy with subject claim `system:serviceaccount:*:*` — any pod in the cluster can assume the role

entries.concept: IAM monitoring, anomaly detection, and key compromise response
entries.description: Even a perfect policy can be defeated by a stolen credential. Production accounts must continuously monitor for suspicious IAM activity and have a rehearsed compromise-response playbook. AWS GuardDuty produces high-fidelity findings (CredentialAccess, Discovery, Persistence) and Access Analyzer surfaces external access and unused permissions.
decision_rules: ENABLE GuardDuty in all accounts and regions; route findings to Security Hub and a SIEM
ENABLE IAM Access Analyzer (external access + unused access); review unused permissions quarterly
ENABLE CloudTrail (org trail, multi-region, log file validation, S3 with object lock)
ALERT on: root login, MFA disable, IAM user creation, access key creation, AssumeRole from a new source IP/ASN, console login without MFA
ROTATE on compromise: deactivate the credential, invalidate all sessions (sts:RevokeOlderSessions), audit CloudTrail for actions taken with the credential
PRACTICE the runbook quarterly — credential compromise drills surface gaps before incidents
tradeoffs: GuardDuty: high signal but ~$1-5/account/day baseline; turn on in every account anyway
Aggressive alerting: catches real incidents but generates noise — tune in the first 30 days
Session revocation: fast containment but can disrupt ongoing legitimate work
anti_patterns: Treating a leaked access key as 'just rotate the key' — the attacker may have created backdoor users, roles, or trust policies in the meantime
Disabling CloudTrail in dev accounts to save cost — those accounts are the easiest pivot point into prod
No alerting on root account use — root use should be vanishingly rare and always investigated
Storing CloudTrail logs in the same account being audited — an attacker with admin can delete them
